hints: Look at the $C=C$ double bond in monomer W and think about what happens to that pi bond when alkenes join to form a long chain.
Keep the two side groups, $CN$ and $CO_2CH_3$, attached to the same carbon and show how the backbone links to the next identical unit with bonds through the ends.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Picture monomer W as $H_2C=C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)$. When addition polymerisation happens, the pi part of the $C=C$ breaks and each carbon gains one new single bond to its neighbour. So $H_2C=$ becomes $-CH_2-$ and the substituted carbon becomes $-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)-$. Nothing is lost, the side groups stay exactly where they were.

Build two units joined together**
Now link them head to tail to make the chain: $-CH_2-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)-CH_2-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)-$. Draw the backbone as four single $C-C$ bonds in a zigzag, put two H atoms on each $CH_2$, and put one $CN$ and one $C(=O)OCH_3$ on each substituted carbon. Finish with short continuation bonds sticking out of both ends to show the chain goes on.

Final answer: Addition polymer section showing two repeat units:
$-[CH_2-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)]-[CH_2-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)]-$ with continuation bonds at each end. The $C=C$ becomes $C-C$ single bonds, $CH_2$ and $C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)$ alternate along the backbone.

hints: Check whether monomer W has a $C=C$ double bond and whether any small molecule like water is lost when it joins up.
walkthrough:
Spot the clue for addition**
Monomer W is an alkene, $H_2C=C<$. It simply adds across the double bond to join the chain with no other product lost. That is the classic signature of addition polymerisation, not condensation which would need two different functional groups and loss of water or HCl.

hints: Scan the polymer side chains for very electronegative atoms and polar bonds that could attract polar groups on another surface.
Remember that N and O with lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds even when the polymer has no O-H or N-H donors itself, and that all hydrocarbon parts always show London forces.
walkthrough:
Find the polar sticky spots**
Look at what the polymer carries on every repeat unit: a nitrile $C\equiv N$ and an ester $CO_2CH_3$ with $C=O$ and $C-O$. Both N and O are much more electronegative than C, so these bonds are strongly polar with permanent dipoles. They can line up with polar bonds or charges on the surface of the object being glued, giving permanent dipole-dipole attraction.

Pick a second force that fits**
You have two good choices for the second row. The lone pairs on the nitrile N and the carbonyl O can accept hydrogen bonds from any $O-H$ or $N-H$ groups on wood, skin, paper or other surfaces. At the same time, the $CH_3$ groups, the carbon chains and indeed all the electron clouds give London dispersion forces with any nearby surface. Name any two distinct types and link each clearly to the atoms or groups above.

hints: Compare X, $CH_3COCO_2H$, with final W and work out which functional group must be protected as a methyl ester before the ketone reacts.
Think about what classic reaction a ketone undergoes with $HCN$ and what new $C-C$ and $C-OH$ bonds appear in the product.
walkthrough:
Deduce Y as the methyl ester**
Start from X, $CH_3-C(=O)-C(=O)-OH$, which has a ketone plus a carboxylic acid. The final product W has $CO_2CH_3$ instead of $CO_2H$, so step 1 must be esterification. Y therefore keeps the ketone untouched: $CH_3-C(=O)-C(=O)-OCH_3$, formula $C_4H_6O_3$ as given. That matches perfectly.

Deduce Z as the cyanohydrin**
Step 2 converts the ketone $C=O$ into the precursor of the $C=C$ in W. The classic route is addition of $HCN$ to a ketone to give a cyanohydrin. The carbonyl carbon gains both $OH$ and $CN$: $CH_3-C(OH)(CN)-CO_2CH_3$. This is Z, which can then lose water in step 3 to give $H_2C=C(CN)CO_2CH_3$, which is W.

Final answer: Y is methyl 2-oxopropanoate: $CH_3COCO_2CH_3$
Z is methyl 2-cyano-2-hydroxypropanoate: $CH_3C(OH)(CN)CO_2CH_3$

hints: Recall the standard alcohol plus acid catalyst needed to turn a carboxylic acid into a methyl ester.
Recall the specific trace catalyst that speeds up addition of $HCN$ to carbonyls.
Think about how a tertiary alcohol with a neighbouring $CH_3$ group can be dehydrated to form an alkene.
Remember that dehydration to an alkene needs strong acid or hot alumina, not oxidation or reduction conditions.
walkthrough:
Choose esterification conditions**
To make the methyl ester Y from acid X you need methanol, $CH_3OH$, with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ as catalyst and warm gently. The equation is $CH_3COCO_2H + CH_3OH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COCO_2CH_3 + H_2O$. The acid protonates the carbonyl and removes water to drive the equilibrium.

Choose cyanohydrin conditions**
Ketones react slowly with $HCN$ alone, so you add a trace of cyanide, $NaCN$ or $KCN$, or a little $OH^-$. The $CN^-$ is the real nucleophile that attacks the ketone carbon: $$CH_3COCO_2CH_3 + HCN \rightarrow CH_3C(OH)(CN)CO_2CH_3$$ Keep it cold to favour addition and avoid side reactions.

Choose dehydration conditions**
Z is a tertiary alcohol, $CH_3-C(OH)(CN)-$, next to no H on that carbon but with three H atoms on the $CH_3$. Strong heating with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ or passing over hot $Al_2O_3$ removes $H_2O$ between the $OH$ and one $C-H$ to give the alkene: $$CH_3C(OH)(CN)CO_2CH_3 \rightarrow H_2C=C(CN)CO_2CH_3 + H_2O$$ That alkene is exactly monomer W.
